title: Child's LEGO stamp: nanoimprint the three most periodic array layers
idea: A child asks why you photograph the same honeycomb billions of times instead of stamping it. Replace EUV on the most periodic array layers (active-area lines, buried wordline, storage-node landing-pad holes) with jet-and-flash UV nanoimprint fed by a master-daughter template tree (one e-beam master spawns ~1,000 replicas, each good for ~10k wafers); DUV keeps the periphery.
why: Removes ~3 of 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4); an imprint tool is ~1/5 the price and ~1/10 the power of an EUV scanner; claim ~8-12% lower wafer cost and less single-supplier exposure. Risks: defectivity and overlay at 12 nm.

title: Embargo patterning: i-line stepper plus five spacer doublings
idea: A Soviet engineer denied scanners prints a 350 nm-pitch line grating on a 365 nm i-line stepper, then runs five self-aligned spacer-doubling loops (ALD oxide spacer, mandrel strip, repeat) to reach ~11 nm pitch, cutting lines with one coarse DUV trim mask; each loop needs only an ALD tool and an etcher.
why: Array line layers stop needing EUV or ArF immersion; i-line steppers cost ~$3-5M against ~$200M for EUV. Trades ~20 extra dep/etch steps per layer for ~60-80% less litho capex on those layers; accumulated line-edge roughness is the risk.

title: Biologist's self-ordering pores: anodic alumina as capacitor molds
idea: Diatoms grow perfect hexagonal pores with no blueprint. Deposit thick aluminum over the array, pre-dimple it with a coarse imprint, and anodize: pores self-order into a hexagonal lattice at ~30-60 nm pitch with aspect ratios beyond 200:1, which become the mold for cylinder capacitors (ALD electrode/high-k/electrode inside), with the alumina stripped or kept as a mechanical support.
why: Replaces the capacitor-hole litho layer and the $10M+ high-AR plasma etch with a wet bath; AR >115 attacks the charge wall (fact 1) and capex at once. Risks: registering pores to landing pads, and opening the barrier at the pore bottom.

title: Printmaker's mask-free interference lithography for crossed array gratings
idea: An etching artist makes plates by interfering beams, not by drawing. Expose array line and hole layers with 193 nm immersion two-beam interference lithography, a mask-free, lens-free tool that writes a ~70 nm-pitch grating across the whole wafer in one flash; two rotated exposures form a hole lattice, and one spacer doubling reaches DRAM pitch, aligned through the moire between the grating and a reference mark.
why: No reticles and no projection optics: a ~$5-10M laser-and-mirror tool replaces immersion or EUV passes on periodic layers, with throughput set by laser power rather than stage scanning. Claim ~50% less litho capex on array layers.

title: Pastry chef's mille-feuille: slice deposited film stacks into line layers
idea: A pastry chef makes thin lines by slicing layered dough. Deposit ~10,000 alternating 6 nm conductor/dielectric films (thickness held to angstroms by ALD or sputter) on a carrier, saw the stack perpendicular to the layers into ribbons, polish them, and tile the ribbons face-down onto the array as a pre-made bitline or wordline layer whose pitch was set by film thickness, not lithography.
why: Turns the densest litho layers into a deposition-thickness problem with zero masks, giving sub-12 nm pitch without EUV. Speculative: ribbon tiling and alignment, polishing damage, and contact landing.

title: Farmer's co-op grain elevator: shared toll-EUV hub for new fabs
idea: Farmers don't each own a grain elevator. A neutral co-op owns a cluster of 4-6 EUV scanners sited among several new U.S. memory fabs (start-ups, IDMs, national labs); sealed FOUP shuttles carry wafers to the hub for their EUV layers only, members pay per exposure, and capacity shares are owned like co-op stock.
why: Takes the ~$1B EUV ticket off each new entrant, so a 20k wafer/month fab can start with DUV-only capex, and lifts EUV utilization from ~70% to >90%. Risks: logistics, contamination, and ~1-2 days of queue time per pass.

title: 2050 engineer's reusable parent wafer: kerfless porous-silicon lift-off
idea: A 2050 engineer laughs that we melt polysilicon in a quartz crucible and saw it for every slice. Grow DRAM-grade epitaxial silicon on a sintered double-layer porous-silicon release layer over a parent wafer, run the front end, bond the device layer to a cheap carrier, cleave at the porous layer, and re-polish the parent for ~10-20 more cycles.
why: Cuts prime-wafer and high-purity-quartz crucible demand ~10-20x (Spruce Pine chokepoint) and leaves a thin device layer ready for stacking. Risks: epi defects driving the retention tail, and porous-layer stability through 1000 C steps.

title: 2050 engineer's bottom-up fab: area-selective deposition replaces cut masks
idea: From 2050, deposit-everywhere-then-etch looks wasteful. Use area-selective ALD with inhibitor monolayers (aminosilane SAMs or small-molecule inhibitors that block dielectric so films grow only on metal) to grow landing pads, caps and self-aligned vias only where the layer below already defines them, deleting separate cut/block masks and their overlay budget.
why: Removes ~6-10 of ~60 mask steps and their overlay error, giving lower litho capex and ~10% fewer process days. Risk: selectivity is lost beyond ~5-10 nm of growth, so periodic etch-back cycles are needed.

title: Termite's chemical tunneling: metal-assisted chemical etching of capacitor holes
idea: A biologist watching termites tunnel with saliva sees etching without bombardment. Pattern a Ru or Pt catalyst mesh over a sacrificial silicon mold layer and immerse it in HF/H2O2: the catalyst sinks straight down, digging vertical holes beyond 200:1 at room temperature with no plasma; the catalyst is removed and the holes are lined with electrode/high-k/electrode.
why: Replaces cryogenic/high-AR plasma etchers (~$10-15M each, the slowest step in the flow) with a wet bench, and reaches the AR ~115 needed for >6 fF (fact 1). Risks: catalyst wandering, metal contamination, and stopping exactly on landing pads.

title: Glassmaker's float line: continuous linear fab instead of cluster tools
idea: Pilkington made glass as a continuous floating ribbon instead of cast sheets. Build the DRAM front end as a linear tunnel where wafers move nose-to-tail on carriers through in-line deposition, etch and clean stations (spatial-ALD heads, linear plasma sources) set by takt time, with litho as the only off-line island, so in-line segments have no FOUPs, stockers or overhead hoists.
why: Cuts AMHS, buffers and floor space (~15-20% of fab cost) and cycle time from ~90 to ~40 days; in-line stations run near 100% utilization, so fewer tools are needed. Risks: one station stalls the line (needs bypass loops), and recipe flexibility.

title: Chef's mise en place: bank generic array wafers, personalize later
idea: Chefs prep ingredients before the orders arrive. Build one standard cell-array-only wafer (capacitors, access transistors, bitlines, no periphery) in huge volume on a stripped-down array fab, stockpile it, then hybrid-bond it to a periphery wafer made in any CMOS foundry, choosing a DDR5, LPDDR or HBM-base personality at bonding time.
why: The array fab needs ~1/3 fewer tool types and no high-performance periphery transistors; the periphery (~49% of die, fact 7) moves to cheaper logic capacity; the wafer bank absorbs demand swings. Risks: ~1 um bond pitch per sense-amp group, and paying for two wafers.

title: Gutenberg's fixed type: a single-pattern scanner that prints only arrays
idea: A printer would not buy a universal press to print one page forever. Build a stripped-down ArF or EUV exposure tool with a hard-mounted periodic array mask (no reticle handler or library, fixed dipole illumination, smaller fixed-field optics) that only steps the array pattern die to die, leaving periphery to flexible scanners.
why: Dropping reticle-stage dynamics, pupil flexibility and reticle logistics could cut tool price ~50-70% and raise array-layer throughput ~30%, and is easier for a second supplier to build. Risk: an EUV version still needs the EUV source.

title: Accountant's frozen node: stop shrinking, depreciate tools over fifteen years
idea: An accountant sees depreciation at ~55% of wafer cost while each shrink buys only 10-20%. Freeze lithography at today's node and win bits only by stacking (tiers, bonding) and design (refresh, periphery), running a paid-off copy-exact tool set for 15 years instead of 5 and financing fabs like toll roads.
why: Halving the depreciation share cuts wafer cost ~25-30%, more than a node shrink buys; copy-exact capacity with a fixed tool list builds faster (~2 years) and cheaper. Risk: rivals that keep shrinking; density must come from stacking.

title: Embargo improvisation: helium-free wafer chucks and closed-loop helium recovery
idea: With Qatar's helium offline, a Soviet-style engineer redesigns the etch/deposition chuck: hydrogen-argon backside gas, a micro-channel liquid-cooled ceramic puck and a higher-clamp Johnsen-Rahbek chuck to close the gap, plus per-tool membrane capture that recycles >90% of the helium still used for stage cooling and leak checks.
why: Cuts fab helium use ~80-95%, removing a concentrated-supply chokepoint that can idle tools. Risks: H2 safety, and the lower thermal conductivity of argon demands tighter wafer-to-chuck gap control.

title: Prospector without Spruce Pine: reusable crucibles with continuous Czochralski
idea: A prospector cut off from the one quartz mine refuses to scrap a crucible per ingot. Grow DRAM-grade silicon by continuous Czochralski with granular-poly feeding in a long-life crucible: synthetic sol-gel silica made from fumed silica (any sand plus chlorination) inside a reusable silicon-nitride-coated graphite susceptor, pulling 5-10 ingots per crucible.
why: Cuts high-purity quartz per wafer ~5-10x and escapes >80% single-site supply; continuous CZ also evens out resistivity and oxygen. Risk: oxygen and contamination control for retention-sensitive DRAM.

title: Origami artist: roll one flat DRAM membrane into twenty tiers
idea: An origami artist turns a flat sheet into volume. Pattern one 2D cell array on a strained bilayer nanomembrane (e.g., SiN/SiGe) over a sacrificial layer; on release, built-in strain rolls it into a tight Swiss roll of ~20 turns, so one 2D lithography pass yields 20 tiers, with wordlines running along the roll and contacted at its edge.
why: Gets 3D density (fact 2) from 2D lithography, avoiding 26-tier stack deposition and deep etch; litho cost per bit falls ~1/N with N turns. Speculative: turn-to-turn registration, heat removal, edge contacts.

title: Child asks why break the cookie: wafer-scale DRAM, no dicing
idea: A child asks why you bake one big cookie and then break it into crumbs. Keep the whole 300 mm wafer as one memory: redundant tiles with an on-wafer mesh that maps out bad tiles at test, wafer-level power planes and edge optical I/O, giving a ~1-2 TB rack memory slab per wafer.
why: Eliminates dicing, per-die packaging, per-die test handling and per-die I/O duplication (~10-20% of cost), with yield handled by redundancy instead of scrap. Risks: power delivery and heat across 70,000 mm2, and serviceability.

title: Commodity trader's forward curve: hyperscaler-funded DRAM capacity options
idea: Grain markets finance planting with forward contracts. Hyperscalers buy tradable 10-year wafer-start options on a new fab, prepaying 30-40% of capex at a strike price and keeping the right to resell on an exchange; builders get capital at near-sovereign cost while demand risk shifts to buyers who can hedge it.
why: Cuts the cost of capital, and the boom-bust risk premium in DRAM pricing, by maybe 3-5 points, making $15B fabs financeable sooner and damping 4x price swings. Risks: contract enforcement and antitrust.

title: Plumber's capillary self-alignment: water-droplet HBM die stacking
idea: A plumber knows water finds its level. Drop HBM dies coarsely (+/-20 um) onto hydrophilic bond sites carrying a water microdroplet; surface tension pulls each die into <1 um alignment within milliseconds, then evaporation and one collective hybrid-bond anneal fix every die at once.
why: Replaces slow precision thermocompression/pick-and-place bonders (~1-2k UPH, ~$3M each) with fast coarse placement (>10k UPH) and a batch anneal, attacking the HBM stacking tax (fact 6). Risks: particles, water residue and bond voids.

title: Musician's harmonics: lensless Talbot EUV from a tabletop source
idea: A musician knows a string repeats its pattern at harmonic lengths. Light a periodic array mask with a compact coherent EUV source (laser-driven high harmonics or a compact FEL); the mask self-images at Talbot distances, and achromatic Talbot lithography prints the hole/line lattice at half the mask pitch through a ~100 um gap, with no projection optics.
why: Removes the $100M+ reflective projection optics; tool cost could fall ~10x for periodic layers, opening EUV-class periodic patterning to new suppliers. Risks: source power (throughput) and gap control.

title: Child's Shrinky Dinks: implosion-fabricated nanoimprint master templates
idea: A child shrinks drawings in the oven. Write the template pattern at 10x scale with a cheap laser into an expanded hydrogel, deposit metal or oxide into the written voxels, then dehydrate so the gel shrinks ~10x isotropically to sub-20 nm features, and use the shrunken part as a master for nanoimprint templates.
why: Replaces days of $10M+ e-beam master writing with cheap optics; template cost and turnaround fall ~10x, supporting imprint-based array patterning. Speculative: distortion over cm-scale fields, and edge fidelity.

title: 2050 engineer's cleanroom-less fab: wafers travel only in sealed tubes
idea: A 2050 engineer finds it odd that we filter a stadium of air to protect a 300 mm disc. Link conventional tools with a sealed pod-in-tube network held at vacuum or ultra-dry N2, with load-lock interfaces on every tool, so wafers never meet room air from start to finish and the building becomes a plain ISO-8 warehouse.
why: The ballroom cleanroom, make-up air and HVAC are ~20-30% of fab construction and a large energy load; removing them cuts build cost ~15-25% and build time. Risks: standardizing tool interfaces, and contamination inside the tubes.

title: Havana mechanic: revive mothballed fabs and stack proven old-node dies
idea: Havana mechanics keep 1950s cars running for decades. Restart idle, fully depreciated 300 mm 2x-nm DRAM and logic lines, including U.S. ones, to make proven 8 Gb DDR4-class dies, then hybrid-bond 8-16 of them into high-capacity stacks for CXL capacity memory, where bandwidth matters less.
why: Capex per GB near zero with mature yields, and it frees leading-edge wafers for HBM; bits per wafer are ~2-3x worse, but capital is ~1/10. Risks: power per bit and stacking cost.

title: TV maker's view: DRAM gain-cell tiles on idle Gen-10.5 display lines
idea: A display engineer notes that LCD/OLED fabs already process 9 m2 glass at <=350 C with oxide-TFT tools, and many sit idle. Add panel-scale nanoimprint for ~100 nm features, build 2T0C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell arrays at <=350 C on Gen-10.5 glass, and cut them into memory tiles for CXL far memory, attaching periphery chiplets.
why: At F=100 nm and 8F2, one panel holds ~15 TB of raw cells, with capex per m2 ~50-100x below a wafer fab: a possible <$1/GB capacity tier. High risk: imprint overlay on large glass with thermal expansion, and speed of long panel wires.

title: Newspaper pressman: roll-to-roll gain-cell memory sheets on steel foil
idea: A pressman prints kilometers of paper per hour. Run planarized stainless or Invar foil through a roll-to-roll line of atmospheric spatial-ALD heads (<=250 C), roll-to-roll UV nanoimprint and web plasma etch to build oxide-semiconductor gain-cell sheets, then cut and laminate the sheets into memory slabs.
why: Continuous web processing at meters per minute could cut capex per bit ~10x for capacity memory, with no wafers, crucibles or EUV. High risk: imprint overlay on a moving, stretching web, and particle defects.

title: Embargo engineer: BEOL-only memory tiers on existing U.S. logic lines
idea: With no front-end DRAM fab available, use only back-end tools that every mature logic fab already owns (PVD, PECVD, Cu damascene, <=400 C forming-gas anneal) to add 4-8 tiers of oxide-semiconductor 3T gain cells over finished 28-65 nm U.S. logic wafers, whose logic doubles as the periphery.
why: Converts underused U.S. mature-node BEOL capacity into memory with a ~$100-300M retrofit instead of a $15B fab, lifting U.S. manufacturability from 1-2% share. Risk: density and retention trail 1c DRAM, which is acceptable for embedded and near memory.

title: Oyster's trick: hydrothermal perovskite capacitor dielectric grown at 150 C
idea: A marine biologist notes that shells grow ceramics in cold seawater. Line the capacitor holes with ALD TiO2, then convert it in place to crystalline SrTiO3 or BaTiO3 by hydrothermal reaction in Sr(OH)2/Ba(OH)2 solution at 120-200 C, skipping the 600-700 C crystallization anneal.
why: Targets k ~70-150 (fact 1 needs k ~70), raising Cs without more AR, in a wet bath rather than anneal tools, and suits stacked tiers. High risk: crystallinity below 8 nm, leakage, and carbonate contamination.

title: Chef's pressure cooker: supercritical CO2 metal electrodes for deep holes
idea: A pressure cooker reaches where dry heat cannot. Deposit Ru, Cu or Ni electrodes from organometallic precursors dissolved in supercritical CO2 at ~150-250 C and ~15 MPa, reduced by H2 at the surface; the zero-surface-tension fluid coats the bottoms of 100:1+ holes and trenches evenly.
why: Gives conformal electrodes at AR >100 without high-temperature CVD TiN, enabling taller capacitors and fewer steps; scCO2 reactors are simple pressure vessels, cheaper than ALD clusters. Risks: precursor purity, carbon pickup, throughput.

title: Frugal homesteader: implant-free junctionless fab with no furnaces
idea: A homesteader without tractors designs around the missing tool. Make every transistor in the memory tiers junctionless or Schottky-contacted (as-deposited doped oxide or poly channels thinned for off-state, metal-silicide contacts), so no dopant-activation anneal is ever needed and the fab owns no ion implanters, diffusion furnaces or RTP.
why: Implanters and furnaces are ~10-15% of front-end capex and many steps; a <=400 C, implant-free tool list (~25 vs ~45 tool types) cuts capital and opens the market to non-semiconductor tool vendors. Risk: junctionless off-current tail vs refresh (fact 3).

title: Jeweler's plating bath: tungsten-free electroless cobalt or ruthenium wordlines
idea: A jeweler plates gold in a beaker at 60 C. Replace CVD TiN/W buried and stacked wordlines with seed-activated, bottom-up electroless Co or Ru fill from aqueous baths at <90 C, densified at <=350 C.
why: Removes tungsten (China ~80%) and WF6 chemistry, swaps ~$5M CVD chambers for wet cells, and lowers line resistance, since Co and Ru scale better than W below 20 nm. Risks: void-free fill and electromigration.

title: 2050 engineer: confined-nucleation MoS2 grown at 300 C as access transistors
idea: A 2050 engineer grows channels instead of etching them. Low-temperature MOCVD (<=350 C) of monolayer MoS2 or WSe2 inside litho-defined pockets that confine nucleation to one grain per pocket forms the access transistors of each stacked memory tier, grown tier by tier within the BEOL thermal budget.
why: A ~1.8-2 eV gap and an atomically thin channel could push leakage below 1 fA (fact 3), relaxing refresh, while tiers grow sequentially with no bonding. High risk: contact resistance, and low-temperature film quality.

title: Metallurgist's layer exchange: aluminum-induced crystalline germanium periphery at 350 C
idea: Old metallurgists knew metals dissolve and reprecipitate semiconductors. Stack amorphous Ge over thin Al with a native-oxide barrier; at 300-350 C the Ge diffuses through the Al and recrystallizes beneath it as large-grain (>10 um), (111)-oriented film, giving high-mobility sense-amp and decoder transistors in tiers above the array.
why: Moves the periphery (49% of die, fact 7) above the array within 400 C, shrinking die area ~30-40% with no second front-end wafer. High risk: Al residue, grain-boundary leakage, threshold variation.

title: Bookbinder's peel: room-temperature spalled single-crystal silicon tiers
idea: A bookbinder peels sheets rather than sawing them. A stressed nickel film peels a ~5-10 um single-crystal silicon sheet off a donor at room temperature (controlled spalling); plasma-activated oxide bonding (<=300 C) places it, CMP thins it to ~100 nm, and a tier of Schottky NiSi source/drain transistors (<=400 C) is built; this repeats per tier, with the donor reused.
why: Gives monocrystalline access transistors on every tier without the 400-500 C split anneal of Smart Cut, and donor reuse cuts wafer use. High risk: spall roughness, thinning uniformity, low-temperature gate-dielectric quality.

title: Cell biologist's membranes: block-copolymer self-assembly below 250 C
idea: Cell membranes self-organize into 4 nm bilayers with no instructions. Coat a high-chi silicon-containing block copolymer (e.g., PS-b-PDMS) into coarse DUV guide trenches; a 200-250 C thermal or solvent-vapor anneal self-assembles 8-10 nm half-pitch hole and line arrays, which transfer as hard masks for array layers.
why: Replaces 2-3 EUV or quad-patterning passes with a ~$2M coater and hotplate, all inside 400 C. Risks: defect density (target <0.01/cm2) and placement error.

title: Child's toothpaste squeeze: liquid-metal-printed atomically thin oxide channels
idea: A child squeezes toothpaste onto glass. Touch a droplet of low-melting In-Sn or gallium alloy (<160 C) to the wafer and wipe: its self-limiting 1-3 nm oxide skin transfers as a continuous InOx or Ga2O3 channel sheet with no vacuum sputter tool, and a <=300 C anneal sets carrier density.
why: Makes ultra-thin, low-leakage oxide channels for gain cells at ~1% of sputter-tool cost, and thinner channels improve off-state. High risk: uniformity at 300 mm, and metal-droplet residue.

title: Military logistician: containerized sub-400 C memory micro-fabs shipped to sites
idea: A logistician ships capability in boxes. Because a <=400 C flow needs no furnaces, epi or implanters, pack a complete memory-tier line (sputter, PE-ALD, imprint stepper, etch, wet clean, metrology) into ~20 mini-environment 40-ft containers that deploy beside packaging plants or logic fabs and add tiers to purchased CMOS wafers.
why: Mass-produced modules could bring capex to ~$200-500M per 10k wafers/month, deploy in 6-12 months and spread U.S. manufacturing. Risks: contamination control and yield at container scale.

title: Quilter's patchwork: collective nanotwinned-copper die bonding at 200 C
idea: A quilter sews all the patches at once. Stack memory dies on (111)-oriented nanotwinned copper pads, which bond by fast surface diffusion at 150-200 C: tack-place a whole wafer of die stacks quickly, then bond them all in one batch press.
why: A lower bond temperature reduces warpage and allows thinner dies; batch bonding raises stacking throughput ~5-10x and cuts bonder count, attacking the HBM stacking cost (fact 6). Risks: pad planarity and voids at <5 um pitch.

title: Sticker-book kid: micro-transfer-print periphery chiplets onto low-T arrays
idea: A kid peels finished stickers onto a page. Make sense-amp and decoder chiplets (~100x100 um) in a cheap mature CMOS fab, release them by undercut, pick thousands at once with an elastomer stamp using kinetic adhesion, and print them onto the <=400 C memory-array wafer or panel, wired by one BEOL redistribution layer; the memory fab itself never exceeds 400 C.
why: Splits the high-temperature periphery (49% of die) from the low-temperature arrays so each runs on its cheapest line; one stamp moves ~10k chiplets per cycle. Risk: ~1 um placement accuracy limits connection density.

title: Alien's question: grow memory tiers on the processor wafer's backside
idea: An alien asks why memory and compute come from different factories. After a GPU wafer finishes its front side and backside power network, deposit 4-16 tiers of <=400 C oxide-semiconductor gain-cell memory straight onto the backside, joined by nano-TSVs and built with the same backside tool set.
why: No separate memory wafer and no HBM stacking or interposer (facts 5, 6); wires ~10x shorter, maybe ~0.3 pJ/bit vs 3-4, with memory capex riding on logic tools. High risk: hot logic below worsens retention.

title: Monk's discipline: three-mask memory tier with spacer-defined vertical TFTs
idea: A monk keeps only what is necessary. Build each tier with three coarse masks: vertical oxide TFTs whose channel length equals a deposited film thickness (~20 nm) on the sidewall of a stepped dielectric, with gate and storage node formed by conformal ALD around the step, so 1 um-class lithography yields 20 nm-class devices at <=350 C.
why: Decouples device size from lithography: ~3 masks per tier vs ~10+, cutting litho cost per tier ~70% and allowing i-line tools. Risks: density limited by contact pitch, sidewall interface leakage.

title: Jugaad engineer: indium-free zinc-tin oxide channels from abundant metals
idea: A jugaad engineer builds from what is plentiful. With indium supply concentrated in China, swap IGZO for indium- and gallium-free amorphous zinc-tin oxide (or Zn-Sn-Si-O) sputtered at room temperature from cheap targets, annealed at 300-350 C, and capped with a Si-rich back-channel layer that suppresses the off-current tail.
why: Removes indium and gallium supply risk from every oxide-semiconductor memory tier and cuts target cost ~3x. Risks: lower mobility (~10 cm2/Vs) and bias-stress stability.

title: 2050 atomic inkjet: maskless spatial-ALD print heads write periphery wiring
idea: A 2050 engineer prints atoms like ink. Micro-nozzle spatial-ALD heads confine precursors and a local micro-plasma in a ~10 um gap to deposit oxide and metal only where the head passes, writing periphery wiring and pads (~1-5 um lines) directly at <=250 C with no mask, resist or etch.
why: Removes coat/expose/develop/etch/strip (5-7 steps) on coarse layers, perhaps ~30% of all patterning steps, using cheap modular heads. High risk: throughput and micron-scale resolution.

title: Battery chemist: room-temperature electrochemical ALD electrodes in capacitor holes
idea: A battery chemist grows metal one atomic layer at a time. Use electrochemical ALD: deposit an underpotential monolayer (Cu or Pb), galvanically swap it for Pt or Ru, and repeat, so electrodes grow conformally in 200:1 capacitor holes from aqueous solution at room temperature.
why: Gives conformal electrodes without vacuum ALD chambers (~$4M vs ~$0.5M electrochemical cell), enabling deeper capacitors at lower capex. High risk: minutes per nm, and uneven potential deep in holes.

title: Temporary-tattoo decal: freestanding perovskite membranes as capacitor dielectric
idea: A child applies a temporary tattoo. A materials supplier grows single-crystal SrTiO3 or BaTiO3 on a water-soluble Sr3Al2O6 sacrificial layer; dissolving that layer frees the membrane, which the memory fab laminates like a decal onto planar stacked-tier capacitors and bonds at <=300 C.
why: Bulk-like k >100-300 gives ~5 fF in ~0.03 um2 planar footprints in stacked-tier cells, skipping high-AR pillars (fact 1) while the memory fab stays <=400 C. High risk: wafer-scale membrane handling, cracking, patterning.

title: Sea sponge chemistry: catalytic room-temperature silica gap fill
idea: Sea sponges build glass spicules at 10 C with silicatein enzymes. Tether biomimetic amine or peptide catalysts to trench walls so they polymerize silica (or titania) bottom-up from aqueous precursors at room temperature, filling isolation and inter-tier gaps without voids, then densify at <=400 C.
why: Replaces HDP-CVD and spin-on glass that need ~1000 C densification, along with their tools; bottom-up growth fills AR >20 gaps where CVD leaves voids. High risk: film density, moisture, breakdown field.

title: Net weaver: aligned carbon nanotube periphery transistors above the array
idea: A net weaver lays parallel threads. Align solution-sorted semiconducting carbon nanotubes (>99.99% pure) into dense parallel arrays by dose-controlled floating evaporative self-assembly at room temperature, making CMOS periphery transistors (polarity set by contact work function) in tiers above the cell array at <=200 C.
why: Puts fast periphery above the array instead of beside it, reclaiming much of the 49% periphery area with no high-temperature step. High risk: residual metallic tubes, and alignment uniformity at 300 mm.
